title: How do you start conceptualizing a game you plan to build with AI?
author: StrangeLingonberry30
selftext:
I'm planning my first game with heavy AI assistance and wondered: how do you structure the concept phase (story, design language, core loop, design doc, scope, etc) before you start building? Do you follow guides or a specific structure to work through everything before building something? Are there perhaps tools that could help with it?

Would love to hear what worked for you!

comments.author: Any-Blacksmith-2054
comments.body: I just start new voice chat and we discuss with Claude entire concept until it's ready

comments.author: Tri8ar
comments.body:
Hey there, and good luck on your journey!

I've started several projects over the last 3 months, and here's what stuck and worked well for me:

1. **Set up your documentation structure first.** Most agents know the common formats and will suggest one for you. There's no single right structure, it just has to fit your goals: capturing the idea and tracking progress. My bare minimum is a Game Design Document and a Roadmap. They keep ideas from ending up all over the place, and they make it much easier to keep context between sessions or even switch agents and models.
2. **Use local git at least.** Agents work brilliantly with git, and it'll save you a lot of trouble when you need to roll back or test something out. You can get into more advanced stuff like branches and worktrees later, but even the basics will help you keep track of your progress.
3. **Check the MCP options for your engine.** Most engines now have first-party or community plugins that make it easier for an agent to work with them. They'll also save you a decent amount of tokens, since it's a more streamlined way to interact with the engine.
4. **Start with the easiest options.** If you have ideas you need to test quickly, you don't need a heavy Unity/Unreal setup for that. You can iterate in a lightweight engine or even pure Python (agents can write that for you) just to test your concepts. Use placeholder graphics too, which agents can also make for you.
5. **Cut your scope, then cut it again.** AI makes it feel like you can build anything, so it's easy to overscope. Define what the smallest finished version of your game looks like and treat everything else as "maybe later".
6. **Keep a rules file for your agent.** Something like CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md with your project's conventions, art style, folder structure and "don't do this" notes. It saves you from re-explaining the same things every session.

comments.author: IriFlina
comments.body:
use phaser or three.js, prototype the core concept/idea with minimum art assets and minimum/no animations. See if the core loop for a single encounter or level, regardless of genre is even fun conceptually, and iterate on it until you feel like it has enough potential to be a real game. Then document what the final version should work/look like into user stories/features/epics and then have AI re-implement the game in unity/godot/unreal or whatever engine you want for your game.

The reason for this is because AI can prototype features in javascript really fast if you're trying to just test out core ideas.

comments.author: goektasgaming
comments.body:
I have these fundamentals as a strict pipeline:  
Idea -> Concept -> Design -> Prototype/MVP -> Product 
Every of these steps have to be iterated until you are satisfied. And then and only then you show it to the world aka Friends/family. And only If these like it too and most importantly YOU like it, too: show it on the internet.  
Most of my games/peoducts take ~1,000 refining prompts and iterations until i am ready to publish

comments.author: Fancy-Proof-9449
comments.body:
What worked for me was skipping the big design doc and doing two small things instead.

First, a throwaway prototype of only the core loop. Mine was a single HTML file you could play on a desktop. No menus, no progression, just the one mechanic. If that isn't fun for a few minutes there's nothing to plan around yet.

Second, once the loop was worth keeping, a short list of rules that must never break, written as plain sentences. Things like "the arena is the same size on every device." The AI reads that list at the start of every session. It ended up far more useful than a design doc, because a doc describes what you want and the AI will happily drift from it, while a rule is something its work can be checked against.

Story, art direction and scope I let grow out of playing the prototype. Planning those up front mostly gave me documents I stopped opening.

comments.author: TheLastNeonDev
comments.body: mine started from something i just loved, hong kong ever since chungking express. so the idea was a neon sign workshop in a 1996 back lane and everything else grew from that

comments.author: VictorBuildsApps
comments.body:
For a recent jam game the agent started from one sentence: who the game is for, what they get, how long a run takes, and whether it can be built well in the jam's four days. Then it wrote twelve candidate ideas, each with its most likely failure next to it, like "the draft screen feels like a menu". Most of them got parked or rejected, and one was picked.

I still pivoted on day two. The pick came from too literal a reading of the jam theme, a film-studio premise I didn't want, so I switched to a sword-and-gauntlet action game from an older shortlist.
